title: Life and death questions
hookLine: end-of-life care and the death penalty: Christians weigh them differently, all starting from the worth of each life

lines: A FORM IN A HOSPITAL HALLWAY.
cards: A woman sits in a hospital hallway with a form on her lap. Her father can't speak anymore, and the doctor has asked whether to keep every machine running.
Across the city, in a courtroom, a jury is being asked a different question about a different life. For the people in those rooms, it isn't a debate on the news. Someone has to decide.
This week has been asking who gets protected: children, the ground, the poor, every race, the stranger. Today it reaches the hardest edge of that: life and death questions.

teach.b: Start with a line from the end of the Torah.

teach.h: LETTING DIE, OR ENDING A LIFE?
teach.b: Moses, in Deuteronomy, sets the choice in front of the people: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life."
Christians on different sides of these debates can each appeal to that line; they disagree about what it asks. Take the end of life. The Catholic catechism, for one, draws a line.
Stopping treatments that are only a burden, out of proportion to any good they can do, can be right: that's letting a dying person die in peace. Acting to end a life is something it rejects.
Some other churches and individual Christians weigh assisted dying differently, and argue it out with care.
Then the death penalty. Genesis 9 says, "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man."
Some Christians read the first half and hold that the state may take a murderer's life, pointing also to Paul's words that the ruler "beareth not the sword in vain."

Others read the second half, the image of God, and say it's still there in the worst of us. The current Catholic catechism calls the death penalty inadmissible, and other Christians argue against it too.
The answers differ. The starting point doesn't.

teach.h: THE SAME ROOT: EACH LIFE MATTERS.
teach.b: Each side is arguing from the same root: each life is made by God, and matters to God.

how: Christians bring these questions to prayer, pastors, chaplains and church teaching; hospital chaplains sit with families making end-of-life decisions, and churches publish statements on end-of-life care and the death penalty that reach different conclusions.

games.q: what does “life and death questions” mean?
o: hard choices where Christians differ from a shared root
questions about how old the universe really is
debates over whether the soul lives on after death

games.q: life and death — tap the pairs.
p: beareth not the sword in vain
my times are in thy hand

s: all Christians reach the same answer on the death penalty
some hold the state may use it; others, including the current Catholic catechism, reject it.
the Catholic catechism treats stopping burdensome treatment the same as ending a life
it allows stopping treatment that is only a burden, out of proportion to any good, and rejects acting to end a life.
Genesis 9:6 is read on both sides of the death penalty debate
one half speaks of shedding blood for blood; the other grounds it in the image of God.

games.q: Moses stands before the people and sets two roads in front of them. what does he tell them to choose?
o: whatever seems best to each of them.
games.why: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." Christians on different sides of today's debates each say they are keeping that command.

practice: Bring to mind one person facing a choice with no easy answer: a family deciding about care for someone they love, a friend at a crossroads. Keep them company in your mind, without deciding for them.
If you pray, you can use a line from the Psalms, "My times are in thy hand"; if not, simply wish them wisdom and peace.
If a decision like this is pressing on you, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Life and death questions. The hardest choices, where Christians reach different answers while starting from the same place: choose life, because each life matters to God.

orig.note: Hebrew: life (a plural form), the word in "choose life" in Deuteronomy 30:19.

carryVoice: Your line: every life counts. There's a life underneath every one of these arguments. Go gently.
